questions.q: Archaeologists dig up an ancient settlement. They find large grain stores, seals carrying written signs, workshops for stone ornaments and goods from distant lands, but the houses are scattered with no streets, no drains and no planned layout. By the chapter's list of characteristics, what is the best conclusion?
questions.a: It falls short of the definition, since urbanism is missing
o: It falls short of the definition, since urbanism is missing
It is a civilisation, since writing is the most fundamental characteristic
It is a civilisation, since any five of the characteristics are enough
It falls short of the definition, since external trade is missing

questions.q: A museum shows a carving of a dancer, the carving on the wall of a decorated building and a recording of a song still sung at village weddings. In the chapter's list of characteristics of a civilisation, all three are evidence of ___.
questions.a: cultural ideas

questions.q: (a) The chapter says a civilisation needs a productive agriculture. Enough to feed whom? (b) Use your answer to explain why urbanism cannot exist without such agriculture.
questions.a: (a) Enough to feed not just the villages but also the cities. (b) City people do not grow enough food for themselves; the chapter says cities can survive only if enough produce from rural areas reaches them every day, so without a surplus from farming there could be no cities to plan and manage.
s: Part (a): feeds the cities as well as the villages
Part (b): cities depend on a daily supply of farm produce from villages, so no surplus means no cities

questions.q:
Read the statements about the chapter's definition of a civilisation.
1. Goods exchanged within a single city count as trade under the chapter's definition.
2. Metallurgy, as the chapter defines it, means only extracting metals from nature.
3. The chapter says some form of writing is needed to keep records and to communicate.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Kabir claims: 'By the chapter's definition, a society could have farms, villages and a few technologies and still not be a civilisation.' Is he right? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: Yes, he is right. The chapter calls civilisation an advanced stage of human society that should have at least seven characteristics, including government and administration, urbanism, crafts, trade and writing, not only farming. It says the first settled farming groups of the earlier chapter, who developed technologies such as construction, were only 'moving towards' civilisation.
s: Verdict: yes, he is right
All seven characteristics are needed, farming is only one of them
The early farming groups were only moving towards civilisation

questions.q: For a class activity, Riya pairs jobs in an ancient city with the characteristic of civilisation each job belongs to. Which of her pairings is WRONG by the chapter's descriptions?
questions.a: A bead driller in a workshop: trade
o: A bead driller in a workshop: trade
A scribe keeping grain records: writing
A worker who clears drains: urbanism
A singer of old stories: cultural ideas

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The chapter calls the Indus-Sarasvati civilisation one of the oldest civilisations in the world.
Reason (R): Civilisation in Mesopotamia began before the Indus-Sarasvati civilisation.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.q: 'The seven characteristics of a civilisation are not a loose list; each depends on others.' Justify this statement with at least four links, using what the chapter says each characteristic is for.
questions.a: A productive agriculture feeds the cities as well as the villages, so urbanism depends on it. Crafts need raw materials such as stone or metal to be managed and turned into ornaments and tools, and these goods are what trade exchanges. Trade, internal and with distant regions, needs records kept, which is why writing is needed to keep records and communicate. A society with cities, crafts and trade is more complex, and government and administration are needed to manage it and its many activities, including the water management and drainage that urbanism includes. Cultural ideas such as architecture show up in the cities themselves. So the characteristics support one another.
s: Agriculture feeds the cities, so urbanism depends on it
Crafts produce the goods that trade exchanges
Trade needs records, which writing provides
Government manages a complex society, including urban water and drainage
Concludes that the characteristics support one another

questions.q: Differentiate between internal and external trade as the chapter describes them, giving one example of each from an ancient setting.
questions.a: Internal trade is exchange within a city or a region, for example grain carried from nearby villages into a town. External trade is exchange with distant regions or other parts of the world, for example ornaments carried across the sea to another land.
s: Internal: within a city or region, with an example
External: with distant regions or other parts of the world, with an example

questions.q:
Match each find from an imaginary excavation in Column A with the characteristic of civilisation it is evidence of in Column B.
Column A: 1. clay tablets with rows of signs kept in a storehouse  2. streets crossing at right angles with drains below them  3. a workshop full of half-finished stone ornaments  4. fields whose harvest was carried daily into a town
Column B: a. urbanism  b. a variety of crafts  c. some form of writing  d. a productive agriculture

A school exhibition describes three imaginary ancient settlements.
Settlement P: about 40 farming families grow barley; each family makes its own pots; a village elder settles quarrels; nobody writes.
Settlement Q: a walled town with planned streets and drains; bead-making workshops; beads sent to lands far away; signs stamped on goods; officials who organise repairs; festivals with music and dance; fields around it feed the town daily.
Settlement R: a seasonal camp where traders from distant lands meet; records of deals are written down; tents only, no streets or drains; all food brought in from outside.
(a) R lacks the characteristic that, the chapter says, generally includes water management and a drainage system. Name it.
(b) Name two characteristics that P clearly lacks.
(c) Show that Q has every characteristic in the chapter's list by matching each characteristic to a detail of Q.
(d) The organisers want to label R a 'civilisation' because it has trade and writing. Decide whether the label is correct and justify.
questions.a: (a) Urbanism. (b) Any two of: writing, urbanism, trade (P has no trade at all), a variety of crafts beyond home pottery. (c) Government: officials; urbanism: planned streets and drains; crafts: bead workshops; trade: beads sent far away; writing: signs on goods; cultural ideas: festivals with music and dance; productive agriculture: fields feed the town. (d) Not correct: the chapter's definition needs at least all seven characteristics, and R lacks urbanism and a productive agriculture of its own, so trade and writing alone are not enough.
s: Part (a): urbanism
Part (b): two missing characteristics such as writing and urbanism (trade accepted)
Part (c): all seven characteristics matched to details of Q
Part (d): label rejected because urbanism and agriculture are missing and all characteristics are needed

questions.q: A student writes: 'Civilisation is something that existed only in ancient times.' Which sentence from the chapter best corrects her?
questions.a: Most societies today show all these characteristics
o: Most societies today show all these characteristics
Civilisation began at different times in different regions
Mesopotamia's civilisation began about 6,000 years ago
Egypt's civilisation followed a few centuries later

questions.q: True or False? 'Because the Mesopotamian civilisation began earlier, the Indus-Sarasvati civilisation must be a copy of it.' Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter says civilisation began at different times in different parts of the world, and it shows the Indus-Sarasvati civilisation growing where it was: villages in the Indus and Sarasvati plains grew into towns, and towns into cities. Beginning later does not make it a copy.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: civilisation began at different times in different places; here local villages grew into towns and cities

questions.q: The chapter defines urbanism as town-planning and the growth and management of cities, and says it 'generally includes water management and a drainage system'. Interpret why water and drains are part of urbanism and not a separate extra. Give three reasons.
questions.a: Urbanism, as the chapter defines it, is not only building a town but the growth of cities and their management. First, water sources and drains have to be laid out together with the streets when a town is planned, so they belong to town-planning. Second, a growing city with many households needs water for all of them and a way to carry away their waste water, so the need grows with the city. Third, both have to be kept working over time for the whole city, which is the management of a city that urbanism includes.
s: Water and drains are laid out with the streets: part of town-planning
A growing city needs water and waste-water removal for many households
Keeping them working is part of managing a city

questions.q: An imaginary town has planned streets and drains, workshops, trade with far lands, written records, festivals, and fields that feed it, but every family decides everything for itself and nobody organises anything for the whole town. (a) Which characteristic in the chapter's list is missing? (b) Using the chapter's reason for this characteristic, explain why a farming village can manage without it far more easily than this town can.
questions.a: (a) Some form of government and administration. (b) The chapter says government and administration are needed to manage a more complex society and its many activities. A small village has few activities, but this town has streets and drains to keep up, crafts, long-distance trade and records, so it is far more complex and needs someone to manage it.
s: Part (a): government and administration
Part (b): needed to manage a more complex society with many activities, which the town has and the village does not

questions.q: Using the dates on the chapter's timeline, how many years after the beginning of Egyptian civilisation did the period of the Indus-Sarasvati civilisation begin?

Write a three-line description of an imaginary settlement that clearly shows trade, writing and government, but FAILS the chapter's test of a civilisation because of its agriculture. Then explain in one line why it fails.
questions.a: Sample: 'Officials of Port Tamra register every boat in written signs. Its merchants exchange copper for shells with distant islands. Its few fields grow barely enough millet for the farmers, so the town buys most of its food from passing boats and often goes hungry.' It fails because the chapter needs an agriculture productive enough to feed the cities as well as the villages.
s: Description shows trade, writing and government
Description makes the farm output too small to feed the town
Explains the failure by the 'feed the cities too' condition

questions.q:
A museum is building a 4 m timeline wall at a scale of 2 mm for every year. It starts at 4000 BCE on the left. The designer must place three markers taken from the chapter's timeline: the beginning of Mesopotamian civilisation, the beginning of Egyptian civilisation, and a band for the whole period of the Indus-Sarasvati civilisation.
(a) How far from the left end does the Mesopotamian marker go?
(b) How far from the left end does the Egyptian marker go?
(c) Where does the Indus-Sarasvati band start and end? Does it fit on the wall?
(d) The wall cannot be longer than 4 m and the scale cannot change. Should the left end be 4000 BCE, 3900 BCE or 3400 BCE so that all markers and the whole band fit? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Mesopotamia about 3500 BCE: 500 years x 2 mm = 1.0 m. (b) Egypt about 3100 BCE: 900 years = 1.8 m. (c) The band runs from about 2600 BCE to 1900 BCE: from 2.8 m to 4.2 m, so its last 0.2 m falls off the wall. (d) 3900 BCE: Mesopotamia then sits at 0.8 m and 1900 BCE at exactly 4.0 m. 4000 BCE runs 0.2 m over, and 3400 BCE would cut off the Mesopotamian marker, which comes 100 years before it.
s: Part (a): 3500 BCE placed at 1.0 m
Part (b): 3100 BCE placed at 1.8 m
Part (c): band 2.8 m to 4.2 m, does not fit
Part (d): 3900 BCE, with both alternatives ruled out

questions.q: A student argues: 'Writing is the least important characteristic. A society could build cities and trade far away without it and still be a civilisation.' Evaluate her argument using the chapter.
questions.a: Her second claim fails the chapter's own test: a civilisation should have at least all seven characteristics, and some form of writing is one of them, so a society without it is not a civilisation in the chapter's sense. The chapter also gives writing a job that the other characteristics rely on: keeping records and communicating. Trade within a region and with distant lands involves many goods and partners to keep track of, and government must manage a more complex society and its many activities, which records make possible. Her first claim, that writing is the least important, is an opinion; the chapter only asks which characteristic is most fundamental and does not rank them. Verdict: the argument is not acceptable.
s: All seven characteristics are needed, including writing
Writing's job: keeping records and communicating
Trade over long distances relies on records
Government of a complex society relies on records
Verdict, noting the chapter does not rank the characteristics

questions.q: A smith melts copper and tin together to make a harder metal for tools. (a) Which part of the chapter's meaning of metallurgy does this show? (b) Under which characteristic of a civilisation does this work fall, and why?
questions.a: (a) Combining metals (metallurgy includes extracting, purifying or combining metals). (b) A variety of crafts, which includes managing raw materials such as metal and producing finished goods such as tools.
s: Part (a): combining metals
Part (b): crafts, managing metal and producing tools

questions.q: An archaeologist may display only one pair of finds and wants the pair to show TWO different characteristics of a civilisation from the chapter's list, not the same one twice. Which pair should she choose?
o: A drain under a street and a seal with signs
A drain under a street and a grid of streets
A bead workshop and a metal-tool workshop nearby
A carving of a dancer and a decorated building
questions.a: A drain under a street and a seal with signs

questions.q: (a) Why are the people of this civilisation called 'Harappans' today? (b) A student concludes from this name that Harappa must have been the capital of the whole civilisation. Why is that conclusion not supported?
questions.a: (a) Because the city of Harappa, in Pakistan's Punjab, was the first site of this civilisation to be excavated, in 1920-21. (b) The name records only the order of excavation; the chapter says nothing about Harappa being a capital, and a site being dug first says nothing about its importance in Harappan times.
s: Part (a): Harappa was the first site excavated, in 1920-21
Part (b): the name reflects the order of excavation, not rank or capital status

questions.q:
A museum's 'discovery wall' shows these entries, with the site names hidden.
Row 1. 1920-21: the first excavation of this civilisation takes place at Site X.
Row 2. 1924: Site X and Site Y are identified as the first two cities of the civilisation; several more sites follow in the same river plains.
Row 3. Later: major cities are found in Gujarat, in Haryana and in the Cholistan desert, and hundreds of smaller sites.
Row 4. Today: discoveries continue.
(a) Name Site X and Site Y and the country in which both lie today.
(b) Name the major city of Row 3 found in Gujarat and the one found in Haryana.
(c) A visitor says: 'This wall proves that the cities in Pakistan were built before the cities in Gujarat and Haryana.' Decide whether the wall supports her, and explain what its rows actually record.
questions.a: (a) X is Harappa and Y is Mohenjo-daro, both in Pakistan today. (b) Dholavira (Gujarat) and Rakhigarhi (Haryana). (c) The wall does not support her. Every row records when sites were excavated, identified or found, not when they were built. Harappa and Mohenjo-daro were simply the first to be found; the other cities were discovered later, and the chapter says discoveries continue even today, so the order of the rows tells us about the archaeologists' work, not about which city is older.
s: Part (a): Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, Pakistan
Part (b): Dholavira and Rakhigarhi
Part (c): rejects the claim, since the rows give the order of discovery, not of building, and discoveries continue

questions.q: Two maps show the same seasonal river: an Indian map labels it 'Ghaggar' and a map from Pakistan labels it 'Hakra'. A student decides these are two different rivers. Which statement corrects her, going by the chapter?
questions.a: One river, which the chapter identifies with the Sarasvati
o: One river, which the chapter identifies with the Sarasvati
One river, which the chapter identifies with the Indus itself
Two separate tributaries of the Indus that join in Sindh
One river, which the chapter says flows all year round

questions.q:
Read the statements about the civilisation and its sites.
1. The people are called Harappans because Harappa was the largest city of the civilisation.
2. The chapter calls this civilisation one of the oldest civilisations in the world.
3. The chapter places Lothal among the hundreds of smaller sites, not among the major cities.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Anil writes: 'India's First Urbanisation happened around 2600 BCE, when people suddenly built cities on empty land.' Taking the chapter's date for the start of the change from villages to towns as about 3500 BCE, is Anil right? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. He is right that the change from towns to cities happened around 2600 BCE. He is wrong that it was sudden or on empty land: villages in the Indus and Sarasvati plains first grew into towns, from about 3500 BCE, and then, with increasing trade and other exchanges, those towns grew into cities. That is a gradual growth of about 3500 - 2600 = 900 years.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: cities appear around 2600 BCE
Wrong part: villages grew into towns from about 3500 BCE, then towns into cities, so it was gradual

questions.q: Of Rakhigarhi, Kalibangan, Banawali, Farmana and Ganweriwala, all named by the chapter as sites of the Sarasvati basin, the only one that lies outside present-day India is ___.
questions.a: Ganweriwala

questions.q: (a) What made the vast plains of Punjab and Sindh fertile? (b) Use your answer to explain how villages there could, over time, grow into towns and then cities.
questions.a: (a) They are watered by the Indus River and its tributaries, which made them fertile and favourable to agriculture. (b) Fertile land let farming villages prosper and grow; as trade and other exchanges increased, the chapter says, villages grew into towns and those towns further grew into cities, such as Harappa and Mohenjo-daro on the Indus system.
s: Part (a): watered by the Indus and its tributaries, so fertile
Part (b): farming let villages grow, and trade and exchanges turned villages into towns and towns into cities

questions.q:
Match each site in Column A with the description in Column B that fits it, going by the chapter.
Column A: 1. Ganweriwala  2. Lothal  3. Mohenjo-daro  4. Rakhigarhi
Column B: a. a major city of the Sarasvati basin that lies outside India today  b. a smaller site in Gujarat, not one of the major cities  c. identified in the same year as Harappa  d. a major city of the Sarasvati basin that lies in India today

Assertion (A): Around 2600 BCE the towns of the Indus and Sarasvati plains grew into cities.
Reason (R): Trade and other exchanges between settlements were increasing.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.q: A student must pick a pair of sites that BOTH lie in the Sarasvati basin according to the chapter. Which pair should she pick?
questions.a: Rakhigarhi and Kalibangan
o: Rakhigarhi and Kalibangan
Harappa and Rakhigarhi
Mohenjo-daro and Ganweriwala
Lothal and Kalibangan

questions.q: True or False? 'The Rig Veda, where the Sarasvati is first mentioned, describes the river drying up and disappearing.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. In the Rig Veda the Sarasvati is worshipped both as a goddess and as a river flowing 'from the mountain to the sea', a full river. It is later texts that describe the river as drying up and eventually disappearing.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the Rig Veda praises a river flowing from the mountain to the sea; later texts describe it drying up

questions.q: A newspaper reports that a new Harappan site has been found in Haryana this year. Using three points from the chapter, explain why such news is not surprising.
questions.a: First, the chapter says discoveries of Harappan sites continue even today, and only some of the sites found have been excavated. Second, besides the major cities, hundreds of smaller sites have been discovered, so new small sites are to be expected. Third, Haryana lies in the Sarasvati basin, where the chapter notes a high density of sites: Rakhigarhi, Farmana, Bhirrana and Banawali are all in Haryana.
s: Discoveries continue even today
Hundreds of smaller sites exist besides the major cities
Haryana is in the Sarasvati basin, with a high density of sites, named

questions.q: A pupil tries four headings for her project on this civilisation. Which heading uses a name that the chapter itself chooses NOT to use?
o: The Indus Valley Civilisation
The Sindhu-Sarasvati Civilisation
The Harappan Civilisation
The Indus-Sarasvati Civilisation
questions.a: The Indus Valley Civilisation

questions.q: A committee must print one name on a new wall map that shows Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Rakhigarhi, Ganweriwala, Kalibangan and Dholavira. The name must best describe where the sites on the map lie. Compare 'Harappan', 'Indus', 'Indus-Sarasvati' and 'Indus Valley', and recommend one.
questions.a: 'Indus Valley' is obsolete: the chapter says the civilisation extended much beyond the Indus region, as Dholavira (Gujarat) shows. 'Indus' names only one river system, but Rakhigarhi, Ganweriwala and Kalibangan lie in the Sarasvati basin. 'Harappan' is named after the first site excavated and says nothing about where the sites lie. 'Indus-Sarasvati' (or Sindhu-Sarasvati) names both river systems along which the mapped cities grew. Recommendation: Indus-Sarasvati.
s: 'Indus Valley' rejected as obsolete, with a site beyond the Indus
'Indus' rejected because Sarasvati-basin cities are on the map
'Harappan' tells the first excavation, not the location
'Indus-Sarasvati' covers both river systems
Clear recommendation tied to the map's purpose

questions.q: (a) Through which present-day regions does the chapter say the Sarasvati once flowed? (b) The Indus waters the plains of Punjab and Sindh. Use (a) to explain why many sites of this civilisation lie well east of the Indus.
questions.a: (a) From the foothills of the Himalayas through Haryana, Punjab, parts of Rajasthan and Gujarat. (b) A second river a little further east also supported villages that grew into towns and cities, so sites such as Rakhigarhi and Kalibangan grew along the Sarasvati, not the Indus.
s: Part (a): Himalayan foothills through Haryana, Punjab, parts of Rajasthan and Gujarat
Part (b): settlements also grew along the Sarasvati further east, with an example

questions.q: A quiz card says: 'Rakhigarhi was one of the first two cities of this civilisation to be identified, in 1924.' Show from the chapter that this cannot be right.
questions.a: The chapter names the first two cities identified, in 1924, as Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, both now in Pakistan. It lists Rakhigarhi in Haryana among the major cities discovered later on, along with Dholavira and Ganweriwala. So Rakhigarhi cannot be one of the first two.
s: The first two identified were Harappa and Mohenjo-daro
Rakhigarhi is listed among the later discoveries
Concludes the card is impossible

questions.q: The chapter says the Indus and its five main tributaries water the plains of Punjab, and it explains a tributary with an example. Which pair shows the same relation that a tributary has with the Indus?
o: The Yamuna and the Ganga
The Ganga and the Yamuna
The Ghaggar and the Sarasvati
The Indus and the Sarasvati
questions.a: The Yamuna and the Ganga

questions.q:
Read this extract from a travel blog.
'I drove from Rakhigarhi in Haryana to Kalibangan in Rajasthan beside a wide, dry river bed. Locals call it the Ghaggar and say that across the border it has another name. Every few kilometres I passed a mound with ancient bricks sticking out. A farmer told me the bed was bone dry when I visited in May.'
(a) Which river of the ancient texts does the chapter identify with this river bed, and what is it called across the border?
(b) Why did the blogger pass so many mounds with ancient bricks along it?
(c) She wants to return to photograph water flowing in it. Should she come back in May or in August? Justify, and say what this tells us about how the river has changed since the time described in the Rig Veda.
questions.a: (a) The Sarasvati; it is called the Hakra in Pakistan. (b) The Sarasvati basin has a high density of Harappan sites, including major cities such as Rakhigarhi and smaller ones such as Kalibangan; settlements were built along rivers. (c) August: the river is now seasonal and flows only in the rainy season. The Rig Veda describes the Sarasvati flowing 'from the mountain to the sea', and later texts describe it drying up, so it has shrunk from a great river to a seasonal one.
s: Part (a): Sarasvati, called Hakra in Pakistan
Part (b): high density of sites in the Sarasvati basin along the river
Part (c): August because it is seasonal, and the change from a river flowing to the sea to a seasonal one

questions.q: Analyse how rivers shaped the birth and spread of the Indus-Sarasvati civilisation. Use the Indus and its tributaries, the Sarasvati, and the growth from villages to cities in your answer.
questions.a: The Indus and its tributaries watered the plains of Punjab and Sindh and made them fertile and favourable to agriculture. A little further east the Sarasvati flowed from the Himalayan foothills through Haryana, Punjab, parts of Rajasthan and Gujarat, watering another region. In this whole region villages grew into towns, and with increasing trade and other exchanges towns grew into cities around 2600 BCE. Important cities grew along the rivers: Mohenjo-daro and Harappa on the Indus system, Rakhigarhi and Ganweriwala in the Sarasvati basin. The Sarasvati basin has a high density of sites, showing how closely settlement followed the rivers.
s: Indus and tributaries made the Punjab and Sindh plains fertile
The Sarasvati's course watered a second region further east
Villages grew into towns, and towns into cities around 2600 BCE
Major cities named along each river system
High density of Sarasvati-basin sites links settlement to rivers

questions.q: (a) The names 'Indus-Sarasvati' and 'Sindhu-Sarasvati' look different. Why does the chapter treat them as the same name? (b) Use your answer to explain why the second river in both names matters for sites such as Rakhigarhi and Ganweriwala.
questions.a: (a) 'Sindhu' is another name for the Indus: the chapter speaks of 'the Indus or Sindhu', so both names join the same two rivers. (b) Rakhigarhi and Ganweriwala are the two major cities of the Sarasvati basin, not of the Indus plains, so a name with only the Indus would leave them out; adding the Sarasvati covers them.
s: Part (a): Sindhu is the Indus, so both names join the same two rivers
Part (b): these cities lie in the Sarasvati basin, so the name must include it

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Archaeologists still debate the purpose of the Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro.
Reason (R): Most houses in Mohenjo-daro had no bathrooms of their own.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Meera says: 'In Harappan cities the elite and the common people lived apart, and the common people's houses were badly built.' Is Meera right? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. She is right that they lived apart: most cities had an 'upper town', where the local elite probably lived, and a 'lower town' for common people. She is wrong about the building: houses of various sizes lined the streets, but the quality of construction was the same for small and big houses, generally in brick.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: upper town for the elite, lower town for common people
Wrong part: the quality of construction was the same for small and big houses

questions.q: In a model town built by a class, every house has its own bathing area, yet dirty water collects in the lanes. Which part of the Harappan pattern described in the chapter is the model missing?
o: Bathing areas linked to drains below the streets
Hundreds of brick wells spread across the whole town
A massive fortification wall around the town
Houses of every size built to the same quality
questions.a: Bathing areas linked to drains below the streets

questions.q: A surveyor uncovers one Harappan street running exactly north-south and predicts, before digging further, that the streets crossing it will run east-west. The chapter's description that justifies her prediction is that the wide streets were often oriented to the ___.
questions.a: cardinal directions

questions.q: (a) Which of the proposed purposes of the Great Bath has been ruled out, and on what evidence? (b) Suppose another city had a similar tank but most of its houses had no bathrooms. Could the same reasoning rule out a public bath there? Explain.
questions.a: (a) A public bath for the people, because it turns out that in Mohenjo-daro most houses had individual bathrooms. (b) No. The argument works only because people already had bathrooms at home and so did not need a public bath; in a city where most houses had none, that reason disappears and the public-bath idea could not be ruled out in the same way.
s: Part (a): public bath ruled out because most houses had their own bathrooms
Part (b): no, the reasoning depends on houses having bathrooms

questions.q: A site plan shows a Harappan city with three distinct zones, the middle one a housing area with perpendicular streets, and most building foundations made of stone. Which city named in the chapter does it most likely show?
o: Dholavira
Mohenjo-daro
Kalibangan
Harappa
questions.a: Dholavira

questions.q:
Read the statements about Harappan town-planning.
1. Streets in the larger cities were often oriented to the cardinal directions.
2. Dholavira, like the other cities, had two distinct parts, an upper town and a lower town.
3. Houses in the lower town were built to a lower quality than those in the upper town.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 only
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Dholavira lies in the Rann of Kutch in Gujarat. Using the chapter, describe (i) how Dholavira stored its water, (ii) how its reservoirs were linked and why, and (iii) how its water source differed from Mohenjo-daro's, and what the chapter says about water sources in other regions.
questions.a: (i) In at least six large reservoirs, built with stones or even cut into the rock; the largest measured 73 m in length. (ii) Most of them were connected through underground drains for efficient water harvesting and distribution. (iii) Mohenjo-daro drew water from hundreds of wells made of bricks; the chapter says that in other regions water may have come from ponds, nearby streams or human-made reservoirs, as at Dholavira.
s: Water stored in at least six large stone or rock-cut reservoirs
Underground drains linked them for harvesting and distribution
Contrast with Mohenjo-daro's brick wells, and other sources such as ponds and streams

questions.q: A model-maker lines a brick tank with terracotta tiles and labels it 'waterproofed as the Harappans did at the Great Bath'. Which correction does the chapter support?
questions.a: Natural bitumen, a kind of tar, applied over the bricks
o: Natural bitumen, a kind of tar, applied over the bricks
Steatite, a soft stone hardened by heating, laid as tiles
Bronze sheets, harder than copper, fixed to the bricks
Stone blocks, like the foundations of most buildings at Dholavira

questions.q: True or False? 'Every Harappan city got its water from brick wells, just as Mohenjo-daro did.' Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. Mohenjo-daro drew water from hundreds of brick wells, but the chapter says that in other regions water may have come from ponds, nearby streams or human-made reservoirs; Dholavira, for example, had at least six large reservoirs.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: other regions may have used ponds, streams or reservoirs, as Dholavira did

questions.q: 'The Harappans gave much importance to water management and cleanliness.' Justify this statement with evidence from at least three different Harappan sites.
questions.a: Mohenjo-daro: people drew water from hundreds of brick wells (about 700 counted), and the Great Bath was waterproofed with bitumen and had a drain in one corner to empty it and refill it with fresh water. In homes, separate bathing areas were connected to a larger network of drains that generally ran below the streets and took waste water away. Lothal shows such a drainage system. Dholavira had at least six large reservoirs, built with stones or cut into the rock, the largest 73 m long, most of them linked by underground drains for efficient harvesting and distribution. Together these show planned supply of clean water and removal of waste water.
s: Mohenjo-daro's wells as a planned water supply
The Great Bath's waterproofing and drain for fresh water
Home bathing areas linked to drains under the streets, as at Lothal
Dholavira's linked reservoirs, with a figure
Concludes on both supply and cleanliness

questions.q:
A student's field notes describe two Harappan cities without naming them.
City A: in a river plain; hundreds of shafts made of bricks for drawing water (about 700 counted); a tank about 12 m by 7 m sealed with a tar-like coating.
City B: in the Rann of Kutch, Gujarat; at least six large basins built of stone or cut into rock, the largest 73 m long, most linked by underground channels.
(a) Identify City A and City B.
(b) What job did the underground channels in City B do, according to the chapter?
(c) The chapter says some regions did not rely on wells like City A's. Name two other water sources it suggests, and say which kind City B used.
(d) A heritage board can fund only one model for an exhibit titled 'How Harappan cities got their water'. Should it model City A's wells or City B's linked basins? Justify your choice from the chapter, and say what the exhibit would miss without the other.
questions.a: (a) City A is Mohenjo-daro; City B is Dholavira. (b) They connected the reservoirs for efficient water harvesting and distribution. (c) Any two of ponds, nearby streams and human-made reservoirs; City B used human-made reservoirs, some cut into the rock. (d) Either choice earns the mark if it is justified from the chapter. For City A: hundreds of brick wells were how people in Mohenjo-daro drew their water, the source the chapter names first; the exhibit would then miss that other regions, like Dholavira, relied on reservoirs joined by underground drains for harvesting and distribution. For City B: the linked reservoirs show water being stored and shared out across a city; the exhibit would then miss the wells, the everyday source in a river-plain city.
s: Part (a): Mohenjo-daro and Dholavira
Part (b): efficient water harvesting and distribution
Part (c): two of ponds, streams, reservoirs, and City B used reservoirs
Part (d): a choice justified by a chapter fact about that city, naming what the other model shows

questions.q: Some large Harappan buildings seem to have been used for collective purposes. (a) Give the chapter's example of such a building and what it held. (b) The chapter says the goods in that building were waiting 'to be transported'. Explain why a city engaged in trade would need such a building.
questions.a: (a) Warehouses, where goods to be transported were stored. (b) Goods made in the city or brought in for exchange had to be collected and kept safe in one place until they could be carried away by land, river or sea; without a warehouse they could not be gathered in large amounts for sending to other cities or distant lands.
s: Part (a): warehouses storing goods to be transported
Part (b): trade goods had to be gathered and kept safe until carried away

questions.q: Which find, taken by itself, would NOT support the chapter's statement that the larger Harappan cities were built to precise plans?
questions.a: Houses of many different sizes along the lanes
o: Houses of many different sizes along the lanes
Wide streets running north-south and east-west
Streets crossing one another at right angles
A city divided into a distinct upper and lower town

questions.q: (a) How was the Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro made watertight? (b) How could its water be changed? (c) A student argues: 'A tank that was emptied and refilled with freshwater must have been a public bath for the townspeople.' Judge her argument using the chapter's evidence.
questions.a: (a) Waterproofing materials such as natural bitumen, a form of tar, were applied on top of carefully laid-out bricks. (b) A drain in one corner let the tank be emptied from time to time and refilled with freshwater. (c) Her argument fails: being refilled with fresh water fits any of the interpretations, and the chapter says the public-bath idea is now ruled out because most houses in Mohenjo-daro had individual bathrooms. A bath for the royal family only or a tank for religious rituals remain possible, and the purpose is still debated.
s: Part (a): natural bitumen applied over the bricks
Part (b): a corner drain to empty it and refill it with freshwater
Part (c): rejects the public-bath claim because most houses had their own bathrooms, naming the remaining possibilities

questions.q: (a) The chapter says most Harappan cities seem to have been surrounded by fortifications. What is a fortification, and what is it generally for? (b) The chapter also says the Harappans do not seem to have kept any army or weapons of war. Does a city wall contradict this? Explain.
questions.a: (a) A massive wall surrounding a settlement or city, generally for protective purposes. (b) No. A wall protects a city but is not itself an army or a weapon of war, so a city can be walled and still have no army or war weapons; both statements in the chapter can be true together. A short answer arguing that a wall suggests some need for protection also earns the mark, provided it still separates a wall from an army or weapons of war.
s: Part (a): a massive wall around a city, generally for protection
Part (b): no contradiction, since a protective wall is not an army or a weapon

questions.q: Two visitors compare the ruins of Dholavira with those of other Harappan cities. Which observation about building materials fits the chapter?
o: Most Dholavira foundations were stone; elsewhere, brick
Dholavira, like the other cities, laid its foundations in brick
Only Dholavira used bricks; the other cities built in stone
Dholavira's reservoirs were stone, but its foundations brick
questions.a: Most Dholavira foundations were stone; elsewhere, brick

questions.q:
In a model-making contest, two teams describe their 'Harappan city' plans. Both have got some things right.
Team A: a wall around the city; a raised upper part and a lower part; wide streets running north-south and east-west; drains under the streets; big houses of fine brick for rich families and small houses of mud for poor families.
Team B: no wall; a raised upper part and a lower part; brick houses of different sizes, all built equally well; wide streets running north-south and east-west; drains under the streets; a warehouse.
(a) Name the feature that, the chapter says, most cities seem to have had around them, and the two parts they were divided into.
(b) Point out one feature in each team's plan that goes against the chapter.
(c) Team B wants to say its model is of Dholavira. Name two changes the chapter's evidence would require.
(d) The judges can give the prize for 'most faithful to the chapter' to only one team. Weigh the two teams' errors and decide.
questions.a: (a) Fortifications (a massive wall); an 'upper town' where the local elite probably lived and a 'lower town' for common people. (b) Team A: houses of different quality for rich and poor (the chapter says the quality of construction was the same for small and big houses, generally of brick). Team B: no wall (most cities seem to have been surrounded by fortifications). (c) Dholavira had three distinct zones, not the two Team B shows, and the foundations of most of its buildings were made with stones. (d) Team B. Team A breaks a clear statement of the chapter, that construction quality was the same for small and big houses, and that statement is the chapter's main evidence about how rich and common people were housed. Team B only leaves out a wall, a feature the chapter says most cities 'seem to' have had, so not every city need have had one.
s: Part (a): fortifications, and upper and lower towns
Part (b): A's unequal houses and B's missing wall, each tied to the chapter
Part (c): three zones and stone foundations
Part (d): Team B, because A contradicts a definite statement while B omits a feature most cities only seem to have had

questions.q: Tanvi says: 'Harappan drains were open channels running down the middle of the streets.' Is she right? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says the drains generally ran below the streets. Houses often had separate areas for bathing that were connected to this larger network of drains, which took the waste water away, as the drainage system at Lothal shows.
s: Verdict: no
Correction: drains generally ran below the streets
Home bathing areas joined this network, which carried waste water away

questions.q: B.B. Lal wrote that in Harappan society 'the differences between the rich and the poor are not glaring'. Analyse how far the chapter's evidence on town-planning and houses supports this view.
questions.a: Some differences existed: most cities had an upper town where the local elite probably lived and a lower town for common people, and houses came in various sizes. But the chapter stresses that the quality of construction was the same for small and big houses, all generally of brick, so the poorer families did not live in visibly worse-built homes. In Mohenjo-daro most houses also had their own bathrooms, and home bathing areas were linked to the drains under the streets. So the evidence shows a society with ranks but without glaring gaps in living conditions, which supports Lal's view of 'accommodation' rather than 'exploitation'.
s: Evidence of difference: upper and lower towns
Evidence of difference: houses of various sizes
Same construction quality for small and big houses, in brick
Shared facilities such as bathrooms and drains
Judgement: differences existed but were not glaring, supporting Lal

questions.q: The chapter's photograph shows a large reservoir cut in the rock at Dholavira, 33 metres long, while the text says the largest reservoir there measured 73 metres in length. A student says the book contradicts itself. Using two facts about Dholavira's reservoirs, explain why it does not.
questions.a: Dholavira had at least six large reservoirs, so the photograph can show a different one from the largest. The 73 m figure is for the largest reservoir, and the rock-cut one in the photograph is a smaller one, 73 - 33 = 40 m shorter, so both figures can be true.
s: At least six reservoirs, so the photo can show another one
73 m is the largest; the 33 m rock-cut one is smaller, so no contradiction

questions.q: Two spots are open for a new Harappan farming village: a hillside with a clean spring but thin, stony soil, and the bank of a river. Both give easy access to water. Going by the chapter's reasoning, why is the river bank still the better choice?
questions.a: The river enriches the soil around it, which helps farming
o: The river enriches the soil around it, which helps farming
A river gives far easier access to water than any hillside spring
Rivers guarded villages against the invasions that ended the cities
A river carries away waste water, so the village needs no drains

questions.q: After describing what was found in Harappan cooking pots, the chapter concludes: 'Clearly, their diet was quite diverse.' Justify this conclusion using every kind of evidence the chapter gives, and say how each kind was found.
questions.a: Crops: archaeological findings show they grew cereals such as barley, wheat, some millets and sometimes rice, plus pulses and a variety of vegetables. Animals: large numbers of animal bones found in excavations show they domesticated animals for meat. Fish: fish bones show they fished both in rivers and in the sea. Cooking pots: scientific examination of clay pots found expected residues such as dairy products and surprising ones such as turmeric, ginger and banana. Grains, pulses, vegetables, meat, fish, dairy, spices and fruit together make a diverse diet.
s: Cereals, pulses and vegetables from archaeological findings
Meat, known from large numbers of animal bones
Fish from rivers and sea, known from fish bones
Dairy, turmeric, ginger and banana from scientific study of pots
Draws the evidence together to justify 'diverse'

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Harappans grew only one cereal, wheat, on their riverbank fields.
Reason (R): Rivers enrich the soil around them, which helps agriculture.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q:
Read the statements about Harappan farming and food.
1. The Harappans were the first people in the world to grow wheat.
2. Some farming tools of the Harappans continue to be used by modern-day farmers.
3. Remains of turmeric were found in the soil of Harappan fields.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 only
o: 2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q: (a) The chapter says the Harappans grew barley, wheat and some millets, and rice only 'sometimes'. What does the word 'sometimes' tell us about rice? (b) A student draws a Harappan farm with rice as its main crop. Use (a) to say whether this is a fair picture.
questions.a: (a) Rice was grown only at some places or times, not as regularly as barley and wheat, which the chapter names without any such limit. (b) Not a fair picture: going by the chapter, cereals such as barley and wheat were the regular crops, and rice was grown only sometimes, so it should not be shown as the main crop.
s: Part (a): rice was grown only some of the time, less regularly than barley and wheat
Part (b): not fair, since barley and wheat were the regular cereals

questions.q: Excavators find large numbers of fish bones at a Harappan city far inland from the coast. Which conclusion fits the chapter best?
questions.a: Harappans also fished in rivers, not just the sea
o: Harappans also fished in rivers, not just the sea
The city must once have stood on the coast of the sea
The fish must have been imported from the coast of Oman
The bones show that the city's people did no farming

questions.q:
In a planning game, a Harappan city has 8,000 people, and each person needs about 0.5 kg of grain a day. Each farming settlement that supplies the city can spare 200 kg of grain a day in a normal year, but only 160 kg a day in a drier year.
(a) According to the chapter, from where did a Harappan city's food have to come, and how often?
(b) How many supplying settlements does the city need in a normal year, and how many in a drier year? Name the factor of decline in the chapter that the drier year models.
(c) In a drier year the city still has only its normal-year number of settlements. Work out the daily shortfall. If such shortfalls went on, what does the chapter say the people who remained did, and why did that help them?
(d) A council member says: 'Just add five more settlements from farther away and the problem is solved for good.' Judge this plan using the chapter's description of that factor.
questions.a: (a) From the rural areas: hundreds of small rural sites or villages, and the produce had to reach the city on a daily basis. (b) 8,000 x 0.5 = 4,000 kg a day; 4,000 / 200 = 20 settlements in a normal year and 4,000 / 160 = 25 in a drier year. The drier year models the climatic change that reduced rainfall and made agriculture more difficult. (c) 20 x 160 = 3,200 kg, so the shortfall is 4,000 - 3,200 = 800 kg a day (one-fifth of the need). The chapter says those who remained adopted a rural lifestyle and scattered over small rural settlements, because a rural lifestyle gives easier access to food and water than an urban one. (d) The arithmetic works for one year (25 x 160 = 4,000 kg), but it is not a lasting fix: the chapter says the climatic change affected much of the world, so the farther settlements would also have less to spare, and a further drop in rainfall would leave the city short again.
s: Part (a): from villages or rural sites, every day
Part (b): 4,000 kg needed; 20 and 25 settlements; climatic change with reduced rainfall
Part (c): 800 kg shortfall; people turned to a rural lifestyle, which gives easier access to food and water
Part (d): judges the plan, noting the change affected much of the world

questions.q: Sohan says: 'Big Harappan cities fed themselves; the small villages around them did not really matter.' Is he right? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says the intense agricultural activity was managed by hundreds of small rural sites or villages. Then as now, the cities could survive only if enough agricultural produce from rural areas reached them on a daily basis, so the villages were essential to the cities.
s: Verdict: no
Agriculture was carried on by hundreds of small rural sites
Cities survived only on a daily supply of produce from villages

questions.q:
Match each find in Column A with the conclusion it best supports in Column B.
Column A: 1. a small clay model of a plough from Banawali  2. large numbers of animal bones in an excavation  3. traces of banana inside a clay cooking pot  4. settlements lined up along riverbanks
Column B: a. animals were domesticated for meat  b. the Harappans made farming tools  c. sites were chosen for water and soil the river enriches  d. the diet included an item the chapter calls surprising
For a school fair, students must cook a dish in which EVERY ingredient is something the chapter says was found by scientific examination of Harappan clay cooking pots. Which dish passes the test?
o: Banana mashed in milk with grated ginger
Barley porridge cooked with milk and banana
Fish stewed with turmeric and ginger
Lentil dal with turmeric and ginger
questions.a: Banana mashed in milk with grated ginger

questions.q: True or False? 'Harappan cities must have imported their cotton cloth from other civilisations.' Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. The Harappans were the first in Eurasia to grow cotton, and they wove it into clothes themselves; the chapter even lists cotton among the goods they probably exported.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: they grew cotton first in Eurasia and wove it into cloth, and probably exported it

questions.q: A Harappan farmer's harvest list reads: barley, beans, wheat, peas, cotton, lentils, millets. Using the chapter's crop groups, the number of items on the list that are pulses is ___.

An archaeologist concludes about a new site: 'Its people ploughed their fields, kept animals for meat and cooked with spices.' Describe one find, of a kind the chapter mentions, that could support each part of this conclusion.
questions.a: Ploughing: a model of a plough, like the small clay one from Banawali, or a plough-shaped farming tool. Animals for meat: large numbers of animal bones in the excavation. Spices: residues of turmeric or ginger found by scientific examination of clay cooking pots.
s: A plough model or tool for ploughing
Large numbers of animal bones for meat
Turmeric or ginger residue in cooking pots for spices

questions.q: (a) The chapter calls dairy products an 'expected' find in Harappan cooking pots. Name the three finds it calls 'surprising'. (b) Use (a) to explain what the banana find added that the chapter's list of crops grown in the fields had not shown.
questions.a: (a) Turmeric, ginger and banana. (b) Banana is a fruit, and the chapter's list of what was grown names cereals, pulses, vegetables and cotton but no fruit, so the pots showed that a fruit was also part of the Harappan diet.
s: Part (a): turmeric, ginger and banana
Part (b): banana shows a fruit, which the crop list does not name

questions.q: A museum label reads: 'The Harappans were the first people anywhere to practise farming.' Which correction fits the chapter?
questions.a: They were first in Eurasia to grow cotton, not to farm
o: They were first in Eurasia to grow cotton, not to farm
They were the first in Eurasia to grow rice, not the first farmers
They were the first in the world to use the plough, not to farm
They were the first in Eurasia to keep animals, not to farm

questions.q: Compare the role of a Harappan village with that of a Harappan city in feeding the civilisation, and then analyse why, when the civilisation declined, people went back to living in villages.
questions.a: Villages: hundreds of small rural sites managed the intense agricultural activity, growing cereals, pulses and vegetables, and cotton, with tools such as the plough. Cities: they could survive only if enough agricultural produce from rural areas reached them on a daily basis. Decline: a climatic change brought reduced rainfall and a drier phase, which made agriculture more difficult and could have reduced food supply to the cities; around 1900 BCE the cities were abandoned one by one. Return: the chapter explains that a rural lifestyle gives easier access to food and water than an urban one, so the Harappans scattered over hundreds, if not thousands, of small rural settlements.
s: Villages as the producers, with crops and tools
Cities depended on a daily supply from villages
Drier phase made farming harder and reduced food supply to cities
Cities abandoned one by one around 1900 BCE
Rural life gives easier access to food and water, so people returned to villages

questions.q: (a) How do archaeologists know that the Harappans ate meat? (b) A student says this evidence proves the Harappans got their meat by hunting wild animals. Correct her using what the chapter says.
questions.a: (a) From the large numbers of animal bones found during excavations. (b) The chapter says the Harappans domesticated a number of animals for meat; that is, they kept and raised animals, so the bones are not described as proof of hunting.
s: Part (a): large numbers of animal bones in excavations
Part (b): the chapter says animals were domesticated for meat, not hunted

questions.q:
A class is setting up a 'How do we know what the Harappans ate?' corner at the school exhibition. It has five possible exhibits: a field model of barley, wheat and millet; a field model of beans, peas and lentils; a copy of a small clay plough model; a heap of model animal and fish bones; and a row of clay pots, each labelled with what was found inside it.
(a) Into which crop group named in the chapter does each field model fall?
(b) Write the label for the plough model: where was the original found, and what does the find show about Harappan farming?
(c) Which exhibit shows how we know the Harappans ate meat and fish, and which shows how we know about dairy products and spices?
(d) The table has room for only three exhibits. Choose three that best answer the corner's question, and justify leaving out the other two.
questions.a: (a) The first is cereals; the second is pulses. (b) Found at Banawali in Haryana; it shows that the Harappans made farming tools, including the plough, some of which continue to be used by farmers today. (c) The bones (large numbers of animal and fish bones from excavations) for meat and fish; the labelled pots (scientific examination of clay pots) for dairy, turmeric and ginger. (d) Model answer: the bones, the labelled pots and the cereal field. Bones and pots are direct evidence of what was eaten, and the cereal field stands for the crops archaeological findings show were grown; the pulse field repeats the same kind of evidence as the cereal field, and the plough shows how they farmed rather than what they ate. Other choices are credited if the three exhibits still cover crops grown, animal foods and pot residues.
s: Part (a): cereals and pulses
Part (b): Banawali, Haryana; Harappans made farming tools such as the plough
Part (c): bones for meat and fish, pots for dairy and spices
Part (d): three exhibits chosen to cover the kinds of evidence, with the omissions justified

questions.q: A student says the small model from Banawali proves the Harappans used bronze ploughs. What is wrong with her claim?
questions.a: A clay model shows the plough's shape, not its metal
o: A clay model shows the plough's shape, not its metal
It shows only that every Harappan village owned a plough
It shows that ploughs were exported from Banawali
It shows that the plough was invented at Banawali

questions.q: A student wants to prove from the chapter that the Harappans used milk. Which evidence should she cite?
o: Dairy residues found in clay cooking pots
Large numbers of animal bones at the sites
A small clay model of a plough from Banawali
Settlements built along the banks of rivers
questions.a: Dairy residues found in clay cooking pots

questions.q: True or False? 'Not every food the chapter lists for the Harappans was grown in their fields.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Cereals, pulses and vegetables were grown, but meat came from animals the Harappans domesticated, fish came from rivers and the sea, and dairy products came from animals too, so part of the diet was not field crops.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: meat, fish and dairy came from animals and water, not fields

questions.q: A farmer in Haryana today uses a plough very like the one shown by the small clay model from Banawali. Explain three things this tells us, using the chapter.
questions.a: First, the Harappans made farming tools, including the plough, to work their fields; the clay model shows the plough existed in their time. Second, the chapter says some of these Harappan tools continue to be used by modern-day farmers, which is what the farmer shows. Third, it fits the chapter's point that, although the cities disappeared, much of Harappan culture and technology survived and was passed on to later phases of Indian civilisation.
s: Harappans made farming tools such as the plough
Some of their tools are still used by farmers today
Harappan technology survived beyond the cities

questions.q: An ivory comb, about 7 cm long and of Harappan make, has been found on the coast of Oman. Which conclusion does the chapter support?
questions.a: Harappan goods reached a distant coast, most likely by sea
o: Harappan goods reached a distant coast, most likely by sea
It was made in Oman and shows Oman's crafts in Harappan cities
It is a seal that a trader in Oman used to mark his goods
It shows that Harappan trade stayed within the civilisation

questions.q: A student writes in a project: 'The writing on Harappan seals has been read, and it gives the names of the traders who owned them.' Show from the chapter that this claim cannot be made.
questions.a: The chapter says the seals carry a few signs that are part of a writing system, but that system, and the meaning of the animal figures, are yet to be understood. So nobody can say what the signs record, including any names. What is certain is only that the seals somehow relate to trade activities, probably to identify goods and traders.
s: The writing system is not yet understood
So the signs cannot be said to give names
Only the link to trade, identifying goods and traders, is certain

questions.q:
Read the statements about Harappan crafts and seals.
1. Steatite is a soft stone that would be hardened through heating.
2. The most favoured Harappan ornaments were beads of carnelian.
3. Harappan seals were large stone slabs, each about a metre long.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1 only

questions.q: (a) The Harappans made bronze by adding tin to copper. Which part of the chapter's meaning of metallurgy does this show? (b) Use your answer to explain why the bronze 'Dancing Girl' figurine from Mohenjo-daro is evidence of Harappan metallurgy and not only of art.
questions.a: (a) Combining metals: metallurgy includes extracting metals from nature, purifying or combining them. (b) The figurine is made of bronze, which exists only because copper and tin were combined, so making it needed metal-working skill as well as artistic skill.
s: Part (a): combining metals
Part (b): bronze requires combining copper and tin, so the figurine shows metallurgy

questions.q:
An exhibition panel titled 'Harappan trade' shows three objects without labels.
(i) A comb of ivory, about 7 cm long, found on the coast of Oman.
(ii) A basin 217 m long and 36 m wide at a small settlement in Gujarat.
(iii) A soft stone, hardened by heating, carved with an animal and a few signs, a few centimetres across.
(a) Name the settlement in (ii) and say what the basin was used for.
(b) Which object shows how far Harappan goods travelled, and which shows the means of sending them there?
(c) The panel has no object for imports. What does the chapter say the Harappans imported, and how sure is it?
(d) The curator can keep only two objects for a smaller panel titled 'How Harappan traders identified their goods and the boats that carried them away'. Which two should stay? Justify, saying what is lost by dropping the third.
questions.a: (a) Lothal; it was a dockyard, a structure used to receive and send boats for further transport of goods. (b) The comb (i) shows how far goods reached; the dockyard (ii) shows the means, boats. (c) What was imported is not so clear; it probably included copper, since that metal was not so common back home. (d) The seal (iii) and the dockyard (ii): the seal fits 'identified their goods', since the chief purpose of seals seems to have been to identify goods and traders, and the dockyard fits 'the boats that carried them away', since it was used to receive and send boats. Dropping the comb loses the only direct proof that Harappan goods actually arrived in a distant land.
s: Part (a): Lothal, a dockyard to receive and send boats
Part (b): the comb shows the reach, the dockyard the means
Part (c): imports not clear, probably copper
Part (d): seal and dockyard matched to the title, with the loss of the comb noted

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Harappans used bronze to make tools, pots and pans.
Reason (R): Bronze, made by adding tin to copper, is softer than copper, which made it easier to shape.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: True or False? 'A Harappan seal dug up far from where it was made can still tell historians something about trade, even though no one can read it.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says that although the writing and the animal figures are not yet understood, it is certain the seals somehow relate to trade activities; their chief purpose seems to have been to identify goods and traders, so a seal found far away points to goods or traders moving.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: seals certainly relate to trade, identifying goods and traders, so a distant find points to movement of goods

questions.q: Which pairing of a Harappan craft with the skill it needed is supported by the chapter?
questions.a: Shell bangles: advanced methods, as shell is hard
o: Shell bangles: advanced methods, as shell is hard
Carnelian beads: stone melted and poured into moulds
Bronze: tin added to copper to make it softer
Steatite seals: stone chosen since it never softens

questions.q: 'The Harappans were engaged in a brisk trade.' Justify this statement, covering what they traded, with whom, by which routes, and the evidence found abroad.
questions.a: What: they exported ornaments, especially carnelian beads and shell bangles, timber, some objects of daily use, probably gold and cotton and possibly some food items; they probably imported copper. With whom: not only within their own civilisation, with cities near and far, but with other civilisations and cultures within and outside India. Routes: land routes and rivers, and the sea for more distant destinations, the first intensive maritime activity in India, with settlements on the coasts of Gujarat and Sindh and a dockyard at Lothal. Evidence abroad: Harappan carnelian beads at Susa in Iran and an ivory comb on the coast of Oman. Seals found in thousands helped identify traders and goods.
s: Exports, including crafted ornaments, and probable imports
Partners within the civilisation and beyond India
Land, river and sea routes, with Lothal's dockyard
Finds at Susa and on the coast of Oman
Seals as tools of an organised trade

questions.q:
Match each raw material in Column A with what the chapter says about it in Column B.
Column A: 1. carnelian  2. steatite  3. conch shell  4. tin
Column B: a. added to copper to make a harder metal  b. a soft stone hardened by heating, used for seals  c. a hard material worked into bangles  d. a reddish semi-precious stone found mostly in Gujarat
Ravi says: 'Harappan traders exchanged goods with cities of their own civilisation and with lands outside India, and they sent all of it by sea.' Is Ravi right? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. He is right about the partners: the chapter says they traded within their own civilisation, with cities nearby or far away, and with other civilisations and cultures within and outside India. He is wrong about the route: they used land routes and rivers, and the sea only for more distant destinations.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: trade within the civilisation and beyond India
Wrong part: land and river routes too; the sea for distant places

questions.q: A student reads that Lothal's huge basin must have been a dockyard and asks for another fact from the chapter that fits a sea-going trade. Which fact should she be given?
questions.a: Quite a few Harappan settlements lie in coastal Gujarat and Sindh
o: Quite a few Harappan settlements lie in coastal Gujarat and Sindh
Thousands of small seals helped traders identify their goods
Carnelian, the most favoured bead stone, was found mostly in Gujarat
Harappan traders moved goods by land routes between nearby cities

questions.q: (a) Name the three kinds of routes the chapter says the Harappans used for trade. (b) Use (a) to say which route a trader in Lothal would most likely use to reach the coast of Oman, and which a trader would use to reach a nearby city upstream on the same river, giving the chapter's reason.
questions.a: (a) Land routes, rivers and the sea. (b) Oman: the sea, which the chapter says was used for more distant destinations. The nearby city upstream: the river (or land), the routes used for nearer trade.
s: Part (a): land, rivers and sea
Part (b): sea for distant Oman, river or land for the nearby city

questions.q: A student sorts Harappan exports by how sure the chapter is about each. Which sorting matches the chapter's wording?
o: Stated: ornaments, timber; probably: gold, cotton; possibly: food items
Stated: ornaments, gold; probably: timber, cotton; possibly: food items
Stated: ornaments, timber; probably: copper, cotton; possibly: gold
Stated: timber, cotton; probably: ornaments, gold; possibly: some food items
questions.a: Stated: ornaments, timber; probably: gold, cotton; possibly: food items

questions.q: (a) Why did making conch-shell bangles require sophisticated techniques? (b) What does the export of such bangles and carnelian beads tell us about the link between Harappan crafts and trade?
questions.a: (a) Shell is a hard material, so cutting and shaping it into bangles was difficult. (b) Skilled craftspeople produced prized goods, and these finished ornaments were among the most favoured exports, so crafts supplied the goods that trade carried away.
s: Part (a): shell is hard to work
Part (b): crafted ornaments were the prized exports, so crafts fed trade

questions.q: Carnelian is found mostly in Gujarat. A carnelian bead of Harappan make dug up at Susa, in present-day Iran, is therefore evidence of ___ trade.
questions.a: external

questions.q:
At a craft fair in Gujarat, a bead-maker tells visitors: 'I start with a reddish semi-precious stone from this region. The hardest part is the work I do on it before it can be worn. My best beads are bought by traders who take them to other countries.'
(a) Name the stone, and say what the chapter says Harappan craftspeople developed special techniques to do to such beads.
(b) Name one other Harappan craft that the chapter says needed sophisticated techniques, and give its reason.
(c) A student says that Harappan beads like these are evidence only of crafts, not of trade. Judge her view using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Carnelian; they developed special techniques to drill the beads so a string could pass through them, and to decorate them in various ways. (b) Working conch shells into shell bangles, which requires sophisticated techniques as shell is a hard material. (c) Her view is incomplete: the beads are evidence of both. Making them needed special techniques developed by Harappan craftspeople (crafts), and carnelian beads were the most favoured ornaments they exported, with Harappan carnelian beads excavated at Susa in present-day Iran (trade).
s: Part (a): carnelian, drilled and decorated
Part (b): shell bangles, because shell is hard
Part (c): both crafts and trade, with the special techniques and the Susa find

questions.q: Compare the evidence of Harappan trade found inside the civilisation's own lands with the evidence found outside it. Then analyse which kind better proves that Harappan goods travelled long distances.
questions.a: Inside: thousands of small steatite seals used to identify traders and goods; quite a few settlements on the coasts of Gujarat and Sindh; the huge dockyard at Lothal, 217 m by 36 m, to receive and send boats. Outside: Harappan carnelian beads excavated at Susa in present-day Iran, and an ivory comb about 7 cm long found on the coast of Oman. The inside evidence shows the means and organisation of trade, but it could serve nearby trade too. The outside finds show that Harappan objects actually arrived in distant lands. So the finds abroad are the better proof of long-distance travel, while the dockyard and seals show how such trade was managed.
s: Inside evidence: seals and coastal settlements
Inside evidence: the Lothal dockyard
Outside evidence: beads at Susa and comb in Oman
Inside evidence shows means, not distance reached
Judgement: finds abroad prove long-distance travel best

questions.q: The chapter calls Harappan sea trade 'the first intensive maritime activity in India'. Give three pieces of evidence from the chapter that support this description.
questions.a: The Harappans used the sea for more distant destinations, beyond their land and river routes. Quite a few Harappan settlements are located in the coastal regions of Gujarat and Sindh. Lothal had a huge basin, 217 m long, that must have been a dockyard to receive and send boats. (A Harappan comb found on the coast of Oman is also accepted.)
s: Sea used for more distant destinations
Many settlements on the coasts of Gujarat and Sindh
The Lothal dockyard for boats

questions.q: A model-maker labels a Harappan chisel 'pure copper, the hardest metal the Harappans had'. Which correction fits the chapter?
o: Bronze, copper with tin added, is harder than copper
Bronze is harder, but they made only figurines from it
Adding tin makes copper softer, so pure copper was the hardest
Bronze is copper with gold added, and is softer than copper
questions.a: Bronze, copper with tin added, is harder than copper

questions.q: Copper was 'not so common back home' for the Harappans. (a) What does the chapter suggest they did about this? (b) If that supply had been cut off, which metal, harder than copper, could the Harappans not have made at all, and why?
questions.a: (a) They probably imported copper in exchange for the goods they exported. (b) Bronze: it is made by adding tin to copper, so without copper there could be no bronze, and so no bronze tools, pots, pans or figurines.
s: Part (a): probably imported copper
Part (b): bronze, since bronze is copper with tin added

questions.q:
A museum gallery on 'The Lives of the Ancients' has six Harappan objects: a bronze mirror, a stone gamesboard, a terracotta whistle, a set of stone weights, the Pashupati Seal and the 'Dancing Girl' figurine. The curator wants to sort and display them the way the chapter does.
(a) The chapter groups such finds into 'objects of daily use' and 'cultural and symbolic objects'. Which two of the six belong to the second group?
(b) Which two objects show that the Harappans made things for amusement, and for whom does the chapter say they were made?
(c) The 'Dancing Girl' is to stand on a 15 cm stand inside a case 30 cm tall. Using her height from the chapter, will she fit, and with how much room above her?
(d) The draft label says her bangles, covering an entire arm, show 'a fashion long since lost'. Should the curator keep this label? Justify.
questions.a: (a) The Pashupati Seal and the 'Dancing Girl'. (b) The gamesboard and the terracotta whistle; the chapter says the Harappans designed games and toys to keep both adults and children amused. (c) She is 10.8 cm high: 15 + 10.8 = 25.8 cm, so she fits with 4.2 cm to spare. (d) No: the chapter points out that bangles covering an entire arm are a practice still visible in parts of Gujarat and Rajasthan, so the fashion has survived, not been lost.
s: Part (a): Pashupati Seal and Dancing Girl
Part (b): gamesboard and whistle, for adults and children
Part (c): 25.8 cm, fits with 4.2 cm to spare
Part (d): reject the label, since the practice is still seen in Gujarat and Rajasthan

questions.q: A tour guide says: 'Since the chapter itself calls this statuette the Priest King, it must show a Harappan priest who was also a king.' Which correction fits the chapter?
questions.a: That is only its usual name; whose figure it is is not known
o: That is only its usual name; whose figure it is is not known
Its inscription names it as a priest, though not as a king
It shows a priest named in the Rig Veda, not a Harappan ruler
It is the three-faced deity seated on a raised platform

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Around 1900 BCE, Harappan cities were abandoned one by one.
Reason (R): Much of Harappan culture and technology survived and was passed on to the next phase of Indian civilisation.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Kavya says: 'The chapter's evidence does not support the old idea that invaders destroyed the Harappan cities.' Is she right? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: Yes, she is right. Long back it was thought that warfare or invasions may have destroyed the cities, but the chapter says there is no trace of warfare or invasion. The Harappans do not seem to have kept any army or weapons of war, so it appears to have been a relatively peaceful civilisation; the two factors now agreed upon are climatic change and the drying of the Sarasvati.
s: Verdict: yes
No trace of warfare or invasion, and no army or war weapons
The agreed causes are climate change and the Sarasvati drying up

questions.q:
Read the statements about Harappan cultural objects.
1. All the cultural and symbolic objects shown in the chapter are made of terracotta.
2. The 'Dancing Girl' is a terracotta figurine found at Lothal.
3. A design on a pot from Lothal seems to tell the story of the thirsty crow.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 3 only
o: 3 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: (a) Using the sizes the chapter gives, how much longer is the stone gamesboard from Dholavira than the terracotta whistle from Karanpura? (b) Neither object is a tool, yet the chapter places both among 'objects of daily use'. Give the chapter's reason.
questions.a: (a) The gamesboard is about 25 cm long and the whistle about 4 cm, so the gamesboard is about 25 - 4 = 21 cm longer. (b) The chapter says the Harappans designed many games and toys to keep both adults and children amused, so play was part of their everyday life.
s: Part (a): 25 - 4 = 21 cm
Part (b): games and toys amused adults and children, part of daily life

questions.q: A student's sketch labelled 'Pashupati Seal' shows a figure with three faces seated on a raised platform, with powerful animals around it. Her friend says she has really drawn the 'Priest King'. Who is right, by the chapter's captions?
o: The student: that is how the chapter describes the Pashupati Seal
